coverageEvidence.excerpt: Consider a fictional five-year cohort of ten people with no loss to follow-up. At year 1, two die without recurrence: eight remain, event-free survival is 0.8 and the cumulative incidence of death is 0.2. At year 2, two of eight recur. Their conditional fraction is 25%, but their cumulative-incidence increment is 0.8 × 2/8 = 20%, leaving event-free survival 0.6. At year 3, two of six die: the death increment is 0.6 × 2/6 = 20%, giving 40% cumulative incidence of death and 0.4 event-free survival. At year 4, two of four recur: 0.4 × 2/4 adds another 20% recurrence incidence. Two people remain event-free at year 5. The five-year probabilities are therefore 40% recurrence, 40% competing death and 20% neither. In contrast, censoring deaths in recurrence-only Kaplan-Meier gives 1 − (1 − 2/8)(1 − 2/4) = 62.5%. Four recurrences among ten with complete observation are 40%, not 62.5%.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A cause-specific hazard is the instantaneous event rate among people still free of every relevant event. Coding a competing event as censored in cause-specific Cox removes that person from this risk set; it does not turn the fitted rate into a recurrence probability. This observed-rate definition does not require assuming independent latent times to competing events. Ordinary loss to follow-up raises a separate censoring assumption. Fine-Gray models a subdistribution hazard linked to cumulative incidence, using a different risk-set construction that retains people with competing events mathematically. A subdistribution hazard ratio is not a risk ratio or a calibrated personal probability. The two hazard ratios can differ without contradiction; choice follows the scientific question, and neither association alone proves a biological mechanism.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A weather forecast is an analogy for updating uncertainty: a starting forecast is revised when new observations arrive. In a trial, the prior describes parameters before the data, the likelihood describes data under the model, and Bayes theorem produces the posterior. The prior, likelihood and target effect must be stated. A 95% credible interval contains 95% of posterior probability under that model. A confidence interval is defined through the coverage of its procedure across repeated samples; a p-value measures compatibility with a specified null model. None is a model-free probability that a medicine works. Sensitivity to plausible priors and likelihood assumptions matters.
